item.title: Police Bill passed by Parliament
item.description: Mansi Chand , Rashika Kumar , Priya Nand , Navitalai Naivalurua , Temalesi Vono , Antornette Vuniuca , Karishma Kumari · 06/11/2026 The Fiji Police Force Bill has been passed unanimously by Parliament which proposes arrest without warrant, use of force by Police officers in exercising powers, provides that any person may make a complaint against a member of Police staff to the Commissioner
item.content:encoded:
Mansi Chand , Rashika Kumar , Priya Nand , Navitalai Naivalurua , Temalesi Vono , Antornette Vuniuca , Karishma Kumari · 06/11/2026

The Fiji Police Force Bill has been passed unanimously by Parliament which proposes arrest without warrant, use of force by Police officers in exercising powers, provides that any person may make a complaint against a member of Police staff to the Commissioner and others.

Minister for Policing and Communications Ioane Naivalurua says t he Bill strengthens the operational capabilities of the Force, while introducing clearer safeguards, stronger accountability mechanisms and a statutory framework for community policing.

He says the Police Bill is more than a legislative update, it is a fundamental modernisation of Fiji's policing framework to meet the security challenges of the 21st century.

The Bill proposes the use of force by Police officers in exercising powers under the Bill or any other Act.

It permits the use of reasonable and necessary force, subject to proportionality requirements and restrictions against force likely to cause death or grievous bodily harm except where necessary to prevent death or serious injury.

The Bill provides for arrest without warrant.

It empowers Police officers to arrest persons committing or about to commit offences, or reasonably suspected of doing so.

The clause further provides that arrest is only permissible where the officer reasonably believes it is necessary for specified purposes, including establishing identity, preventing harm or obstruction, protecting vulnerable persons, ensuring effective investigation, or preventing disappearance .

The Bill empowers a Police officer to enter and search a place or conveyance without a warrant where the officer reasonably suspects evidence may be concealed or destroyed, or where an urgent search offence involves conveyance safety.

The clause provides that the search may be conducted as if authorised by warrant and restricts the use of force in relation to structural damage or forced entry into conveyances.

The Bill empowers the Commissioner to require a candidate to provide a body sample and to allow biometric information to be taken for the purposes of establishing a DNA profile.

Clause 23 restricts the use of biometric information relating to a candidate.

The clause provides that such information may be used only for verifying that the candidate is not an illicit drug user , determining whether the candidate has been convicted of an offence, investigating and prosecuting offences where the candidate is linked through matching, or eliminating the candidate from suspicion if later recruited.

It proposes that any person may make a complaint against a member of Police staff to the Commissioner in the prescribed form and manner.

The clause further requires the Commissioner to establish a complaints receiving and response platform that enables anonymous and user-friendly lodgement of complaints.

T he Bill empowers a Police officer to take identifying particulars of a person in lawful Police custody who is detained for committing an offence.

The clause provides that identifying particulars must be taken in a reasonable manner and permits the use of force, subject to clause 42.

The clause also creates an offence for failure to comply with a lawful direction after caution with the penalty of a fine not exceeding $5,000 or imprisonment for a term not exceeding 6 months or both.

The Bill empowers a Police officer to detain a person briefly for the purpose of taking identifying particulars where the officer reasonably suspects the person of committing an offence and intends to proceed by summons.

The clause limits detention to the period necessary to obtain the particulars allows reasonable force to be used to secure them and creates an offence for failure to comply after caution.

The Minister says t he Bill provides the legislative foundation for these essential standards.

Attorney-General Sevuloni Valenitabua says the Bill addresses several constitutional requirements, including the rights of arrested and detained persons, protection of privacy, freedom of expression and the use of force by police officers.

On search and privacy, Valenitabua says the Bill provides that general or urgent search warrants may only be issued by a magistrate, while covert surveillance and covert entry warrants can only be issued by a High Court judge.

He says Justices of the Peace, who previously had some of these powers, have been removed from that process.

Valenitabua says Clauses 59 and 65 also require judges to consider the seriousness of an offence, the extent to which a person's privacy would be affected and whether there are other ways to obtain evidence before issuing surveillance or tracking warrants.

He says the Bill also removes the old offence of causing disaffection among police officers, with Clause 148 now making it an offence to induce a member of police staff to withhold their services or commit a breach of discipline.

He says the Bill gives police officers modern powers while assuring citizens that those powers are bounded by the Constitution and international standards Fiji has freely accepted.

Valenitabua has commended the Minister for Policing, the Commissioner of Police, the Ministry, the Standing Committee on Justice, Law and Human Rights and members of the public who made submissions towards the development of the Bill.

He says supporting the Bill also reaffirms the nation's commitment to the men and women of the Fiji Police Force and the families who stand behind them.

item.title: Diwali celebrations begin with Dhanteras today
item.description: According to the Shree Sanatan Dharm Brahman Sabha of Fiji, Dhanteras begins at 5pm this afternoon, while the Yam Deep Daan timing is from 5.33pm to 6.51pm. Roop Narak Chaturdashi and Shri Hanuman Utsav will be observed tomorrow which begins at 5.17pm and ends at 5.57pm on Sunday.
item.content:encoded:
According to the Shree Sanatan Dharm Brahman Sabha of Fiji, Dhanteras begins at 5pm this afternoon, while the Yam Deep Daan timing is from 5.33pm to 6.51pm.

Roop Narak Chaturdashi and Shri Hanuman Utsav will be observed tomorrow which begins at 5.17pm and ends at 5.57pm on Sunday.

Diwali will be celebrated this Sunday while public holiday will be on Monday.

The celebrations will continue with Govardhan Pooja next Tuesday, followed by Bhai Duj on Wednesday.
